title: Counterparty Exposure Profiles: EE, PFE, EPE

maps.tested: The sheet says 'various payoff profiles are important, especially security exposure profiles', then flags the netting factor formula as the calculation to know.
maps.specifics: Your formula card lists 'potential credit risk exposure' and 'netting' as separate rows. The examinable set is expected MtM, expected exposure, PFE, EPE, effective EE/EPE and maximum PFE, a six-way sibling family, plus the netting factor. Red-herring risk: a sold option carries zero counterparty exposure regardless of how much Black-Scholes data the stem supplies.

vardeezReading: CR-19: Very Important, "Various Payoff profiles are important" (security exposure profiles), and the netting factor formula and its impact matter (see the Crash Course); LO g, funding versus credit exposure, is to be read. CR-12: Important, but only LO g (credit VaR), LO f (one-factor model) and LO e matter, the rest are repeats to skim, and none of them is a C8 point.

selectors.name: Six-way exposure metric family
selectors.what: Compute or tell apart expected MtM (EFV), EPE / expected exposure, PFE, ENE, effective EE/EPE and average EPE, and maximum PFE, e.g. from scenario values: EFV = average of all values, EPE = (1/n) x sum of max(V, 0) over all n scenarios, ENE = (1/n) x sum of min(V, 0), PFE = the quantile of the exposure distribution at the confidence level, average EPE = time-weighted average of the EPE profile, maximum PFE = the peak of the PFE profile.
selectors.theory: What each metric measures and how they differ: EFV is the mean of all values and equals today's value at time zero; EPE counts zero and negative values as zero (divide by all scenarios, not only the positive ones); PFE is a high quantile like a VaR; ENE is the negative-side counterpart; higher volatility raises EPE, ENE in magnitude and PFE but leaves EFV unchanged; average EPE is the loan equivalent; Basel's effective EE is non-decreasing over time. Acronyms collide, so the definition in the stem decides.

selectors.name: Netting and aggregation of exposure
selectors.what: Aggregation across trades in a netting set: EFV is additive but EPE and ENE are not (aggregated EPE is at most the sum of the standalone EPEs), and the netting factor NF = sqrt(n + n(n - 1) x rho) / n for n trades of equal exposure with common correlation rho, netted exposure being NF times gross.
selectors.theory: Why netting helps only in scenarios where values have opposite signs, since max(sum of v_i, 0) <= sum of max(v_i, 0); the benefit grows with more trades and lower or negative correlation; netting needs an enforceable legal agreement, and without it exposure is the sum of the standalone exposures.

selectors.name: Trap: sold option has zero exposure
selectors.what: The stem gives spot, strike, volatility or a Black-Scholes value for an option the party has sold with the premium paid upfront: its exposure is zero on every path, so the Black-Scholes value is never added to EPE or used to offset another trade's exposure.

selectors.name: Exposure profiles by instrument
selectors.source: Vardeez: 'Payoff / security exposure profiles' (CR-19 d) and 'Security exposure profiles' (CR-19 e); Map: 'various payoff profiles are important'
selectors.what: Identify or compare the shape of the exposure profile over time for forwards, options, interest rate swaps, cross-currency swaps, swaptions and CDS, including how payment frequency and exercise dates change it.
selectors.theory: Forward, FX forward and vanilla option exposure grows with the square root of time and ends at maturity; a swap profile is humped (proportional to (T - t) x sqrt(t)) with its peak near T/3; a cross-currency swap carries a large final notional exchange; payer versus receiver on an upward curve flips EPE and ENE; a physically settled swaption has higher exposure than the forward swap before exercise and lower after.
